1. Use the `Adult Census Income` dataset.  We will predict the income (whether or not it is more than 50k or not) of an adult. Import the dataset.  Partition the data into 80% training and 20% testing.  

```{r}

library(tidyverse)
df = read_csv("https://bryantstats.github.io/math421/data/adult_census.csv")

df <- df %>% 
  rename(target = income)

df <- df %>% 
  mutate(
    target = as.factor(target),
    workclass = as.factor(workclass),
    education = as.factor(education),
    marital.status = as.factor(marital.status),
    occupation = as.factor(occupation), 
    relationship = as.factor(relationship), 
    race = as.factor(race), 
    sex = as.factor(sex), 
    native.country = as.factor(native.country)
  )



library(caret)
set.seed(123)

train_index <- createDataPartition(df$target, p= 0.80, list = FALSE)

df_train <- df[train_index, ]
df_test <- df[-train_index, ]



```


2. Practice Decision Tree.  Do the follows:

  - Use `rpart` package, create a decision tree with maximum depth of 3. 
  
  - Calculate the accuracy of the model on the testing data. Notice that the positive outcome here is not `1` but `>50K` or `<50K`. 
  
  - Plot the tree
  
  - Plot the variable importance by the tree
```{r}
library(rpart)
library(rattle)
#create a tree 
tree_model <- rpart(target ~., data = df_train,
                     control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 3)
  )

# predict on testing data 
pred <- predict (tree_model, df_test, type = 'class')

# evaluate the predictions 
cm <- confusionMatrix(data = pred, reference = df_test$target, positive = ">50K")
cm$overall["Accuracy"]


tree_model$variable.importance
barplot(tree_model$variable.importance)

fancyRpartPlot(tree_model)
```
```
```

  
3. Create 3 more trees and compare the testing accuracy of these trees, which tree give the highest testing accuracy.
```{r}
#tree 2
tree2 <- rpart(target ~., data = df_train, method = 'class', control = rpart.control(max.depth = 6))

pred2 <- predict(tree2, df_test, type = 'class')
acc2<- confusionMatrix(pred2, df_test$target, 
                       positive = ">50K")$overall["Accuracy"]


#Tree 3 
tree3 <- rpart(target ~., data = df_train, method = 'class', control = rpart.control(max.depth = 8))

pred3 <- predict(tree3, df_test, type = "class")
acc3 <- confusionMatrix(pred3, df_test$target,
                        positive = ">50K")$overall["Accuracy"]


#Tree 4 
tree4 <- rpart(target ~., data = df_train, method = 'class', control = rpart.control(max.depth = 10))

pred4 <- predict(tree4, df_test, type = "class")
acc4 <- confusionMatrix(pred4, df_test$target,
                        positive = ">50K")$overall["Accuracy"]

#compare accuracies 
data.frame( 
  MaxDepth = c(6, 8, 10), 
  Accuracy = c(acc2, acc3, acc4)
)
```


4. Practice Random Forest.  Do the follows: 

  - Use `randomForest` package, create a random forest of 1000 trees. 
  
  - Calculate the accuracy of the model on the testing data. 
  
  - Plot the variable importance by the forest 
  
```{r}
library(randomForest) 
library(caret)
forest_model = randomForest(target ~ ., data = df_train, ntree = 1000)
pred <- predict(forest_model, df_test, type = "class")
cm <- confusionMatrix(data = pred, reference = df_test$target, positive = ">50K")
cm$overall[1]

importance(forest_model)
```
  
  
5. Create 3 more forests and compare the testing accuracy of these forests, which forest give the highest testing accuracy.
```{r}
#tree 2 
forest2 <- randomForest(target ~., data = df_train, ntree = 200)

pred2 <- predict(forest2, df_test)
cm2 <- confusionMatrix(pred2, df_test$target)

#tree 3 
forest3 <- randomForest(target ~., data = df_train, ntree = 500)


pred3 <- predict(forest3, df_test)
cm3 <- confusionMatrix(pred3, df_test$target)

# tree 4 
forest4 <- randomForest(target ~ ., data = df_train, ntree = 1000)

pred4 <- predict(forest4, df_test)
cm4 <- confusionMatrix(pred4, df_test$target)

```
